page: Amazon Web Services a1.xlarge is an ARM-based virtual machine instance powered by the first-generation AWS Graviton processor. Built on the Nitro hypervisor, this instance features 4 dedicated physical cores and 4 vCPUs using the ARMv8 Cortex-A72 architecture running at 2.3 GHz. It is configured with 8.0 GB of system memory, yielding a 2.0 GB memory-per-core ratio. The processor includes 32 KB of L1 data cache and 2 MB of L2 cache per core, with no L3 cache. It lacks advanced vector and matrix extensions such as AVX or AMX, but supports hardware-accelerated AES cryptography. The instance does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, and operates with a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

Benchmark data indicates that the first-generation Graviton processor delivers entry-level performance. In stress-ng testing, single-core CPU performance falls within the average range at 1488.48, while multi-core performance is weak at 5919.11. Memory bandwidth is a primary bottleneck, with uncached read and write speeds of 12.56 GB/sec and 6.77 GB/sec respectively, placing it in the bottom decile of tested hardware. Similarly, Geekbench scores are low, with a single-core score of 408.0 and a multi-core score of 1245.0. Software compilation, image processing, and text processing benchmarks consistently rank in the bottom 10% of performance tiers.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the a1.xlarge offers a low-cost entry point into ARM64 development and testing, but presents significant performance tradeoffs. The lack of hyperthreading and advanced vector instructions limits its utility for high-throughput compute tasks. Static web serving throughput is measured at 1.36 GB/sec, and database operations score weakly at 1263.44. Consequently, this instance is best suited for lightweight containerized microservices, basic web serving, ARM64 software compilation testing, and low-traffic development environments where raw execution speed is secondary to cost-effective dedicated resource allocation.
